lead: A describing function replaces a nonlinear element by an amplitude-dependent gain N(A). The input is a sine wave A sin ωt. N(A)=Y<sub>1</sub>/A is the complex ratio of the fundamental output phasor Y<sub>1</sub> to the input phasor A; its magnitude is the output-to-input fundamental amplitude ratio and its angle is the fundamental phase shift. N(A) is real when the nonlinearity causes no phase shift, e.g. saturation and an ideal relay. The linear plant is assumed to pass only that fundamental. A linear frequency-domain test then predicts a limit cycle: plot G(jω) and −1/N(A); their intersection gives the oscillation amplitude and frequency. Engineers use this on saturating actuators, relays and control valves with backlash, where exact simulation is slow and a quick estimate is enough.
prereq: You need: Unit 4 Nyquist plot and frequency response, and 7.1 Common nonlinearities.

blocks.text: The method treats the nonlinear block as a black box. Feed x(t)=A sin(ωt), where A is the input amplitude in volts and ω is angular frequency in rad/s. The output n(x) is periodic but not sinusoidal. Fourier analysis splits it into a fundamental at ω plus harmonics at 2ω, 3ω and so on.

Two assumptions make the method work. The nonlinearity must be odd, n(−x)=−n(x), and time-invariant. For single-valued nonlinearities such as saturation and an ideal relay, it is also memoryless: the output at any instant depends only on the input at that instant. Memory-type nonlinearities such as backlash and relays with hysteresis break the memoryless condition: their describing function is derived over one full input period, is complex, and depends on the hysteresis width as well as on A. The linear plant G(jω) must be low-pass: its gain at 2ω, 3ω, ... is small enough to ignore. Then only the fundamental reaches the feedback loop.

The describing function is the complex ratio of the fundamental output phasor to the input phasor: N(A)=Y<sub>1</sub>/A. Here Y<sub>1</sub> is the fundamental output phasor; its magnitude is the fundamental output amplitude and its angle is measured relative to the input. If the nonlinearity has no phase shift, N(A) is real. For a linear gain n(x)=kx, N(A)=k for all A. For a nonlinearity, N(A) changes with A; this is the whole point. N(A) is not the local slope at x=0. Some syllabi call the method harmonic linearization or the sinusoidal describing function.
Take saturation with linear gain k and limit a. For |x|≤a, n(x)=kx. For x>a, n(x)=ka. For x<−a, n(x)=−ka. Here k is the unsaturated slope, dimensionless; a is the input limit in volts.
N(A)=k for A≤a;  N(A)=(2k/π)[sin⁻¹(a/A)+(a/A)√(1−(a/A)²)] for A>a
blocks.where: A is the sine amplitude in V; a is the saturation limit in V; k is the unsaturated slope (dimensionless); sin⁻¹ returns radians.

blocks.text: At A=a the two branches meet at N=k. As A grows, N falls. A relay with output levels ±M has N(A)=4M/(πA), where M is the relay output height in volts and A is input amplitude in volts. The formula ignores relay hysteresis. Backlash gives a complex N(A) with phase lag; it is not a single real curve.

Set the loop to 1+N(A)G(jω)=0. Rearranged, G(jω)=−1/N(A). The right side is a locus in the complex plane as A varies. On the same Nyquist plot, draw G(jω) for ω from 0 to ∞. Each intersection is a candidate limit cycle: read A from the −1/N locus and ω from the G locus.

items: Write n(x), then find N(A) for the nonlinear block.
Draw G(jω) from the linear part.
Draw −1/N(A) for A from 0 to ∞, with an arrow for increasing A.
Mark intersections; read amplitude A and frequency ω.

Check the crossing direction: for a single intersection, the limit cycle is stable if, as A increases through the intersection, the point on the −1/N locus crosses from inside the G(jω) locus to outside. Also check the ω direction along G(jω). Unstable crossings do not produce a sustained oscillation. A limit cycle is an estimate, not a proof.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call the intersection the describing-function limit cycle. Use it as an estimate, not a proof: harmonics are ignored. See 7.4 Limit cycles for the exact definition of an isolated closed path.

figure.caption: The saturation describing function for k=5 and a=2 V: flat at N=5 while A≤2 V, then falling as A grows. The point A=4 V, N=3.045 is the worked example.

spec.aria: The describing function starts at 5 for small amplitudes and falls to about 1.27 at A=10.

examples.question: A saturating amplifier has linear gain k=5 and saturation limit a=2 V. A sine input of amplitude A=4 V drives it. Find N(A).
steps: Check the branch: A=4 V > a=2 V, so use the saturation formula.
examples.check:
import math
k = 5.0
a = 2.0
A = 4.0
r = a / A
N = (2 * k / math.pi) * (math.asin(r) + r * math.sqrt(1 - r * r))
print(round(N, 3))

traps: N(A) is not the slope at the origin. For saturation the slope near zero is k, while N(A) falls once A exceeds a.
The −1/N locus can be a curve with phase, especially for backlash. Do not treat it as a fixed point on the negative real axis.
The method assumes the plant filters harmonics. If the plant passes 2ω or 3ω strongly, the sine-wave prediction can be badly wrong.
For a relay, N=4M/(πA) uses the relay output height M, not the peak-to-peak value 2M.

quiz.q: Define the describing function N(A) in one sentence.
quiz.a: N(A)=Y<sub>1</sub>/A is the complex ratio of the fundamental output phasor Y<sub>1</sub> to the input phasor A; its magnitude is the output-to-input fundamental amplitude ratio and its angle is the fundamental phase shift. N(A) is real when the nonlinearity causes no phase shift, e.g. saturation and an ideal relay.

quiz.q: Why must the linear plant be low-pass for describing function analysis?
quiz.a: It must suppress harmonics so only the fundamental returns around the loop; otherwise the sine-wave assumption is invalid.

quiz.q: A saturation has k=2 and a=1 V. Find N(A) for A=2 V.
A relay has output levels ±M with M=12 V. Find N(A) for A=3 V.
Why can the −1/N(A) locus be a curve instead of a single point?
quiz.a: For backlash and some nonlinearities N(A) is complex, so both magnitude and phase change with A. The locus then traces a curve in the complex plane.

quiz.q: What does an intersection of G(jω) and −1/N(A) give?
quiz.a: A candidate limit cycle: amplitude A from the −1/N locus and frequency ω from the G locus. Stability needs a crossing check.

beyond: Not for the exam. Relay feedback is used in industry to auto-tune PID loops: a relay deliberately causes a small oscillation, and the describing function estimates ultimate gain and period. Harmonic balance extends the same idea to higher harmonics and to multiple sinusoidal inputs. Search 'relay auto-tuning', 'harmonic balance' and 'describing function stability criterion'.
